procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 9, 1964 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 200 of 1964 and Death Reference No. 9 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Patna accepted the death reference, confirmed the conviction and sentence (death sentence), and dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave after the High Court confirmed his conviction and death sentence.

directions: the appellant is directed to be set at liberty forthwith

issue.issue_text: Whether a person giving information to a police officer, which may be used as evidence against them, can be considered to be in 'constructive custody' under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, even if they have not been formally arrested.

facts: The appellant gave a first information report to a Sub Inspector, which led to the discovery of dead bodies and a weapon (tangi).
The Sub Inspector stated that he formally arrested the appellant only *after* the report was given.
law: Section 27 of the Evidence Act allows information received from an accused person to be used as evidence if it leads to the discovery of a fact, but only if the person was "in the custody of a police officer" when they gave the information.
application: The court noted that, prima facie, the appellant was not in custody when he gave the report because the arrest occurred later.
The court then considered the concept of "constructive custody," which would mean the appellant had submitted himself to police custody even without a formal arrest.
The judgment acknowledged that there was a "conflict of opinion" among judges on whether a person giving incriminating information to a police officer could be deemed to be in constructive custody.
reasoning.conclusion: For the purposes of this specific case, the court decided to **assume** that the appellant was in constructive police custody when he gave the information. Based on this assumption, the court accepted that the part of the information report leading to the discovery was admissible under Section 27.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person giving information to a police officer, which may be used as evidence against them, can be considered to be in 'constructive custody' under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, even if they have not been formally arrested.
appellant_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the appellant's argument on the specific issue of 'constructive custody'. Their broader argument was that the entire statement was an inadmissible confession made to a police officer under Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument on the specific issue of 'constructive custody'. However, their position would have been that the appellant had submitted to the custody of the police officer by giving the information, thus placing him in 'constructive custody' and making the subsequent discovery admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.

cases.case_name: State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya
cases.principle: To show that there is a conflict of judicial opinion on the question of whether a person giving information to a police officer, which may be used against him, can be deemed to have submitted himself to the constructive custody of the police officer within the meaning of s. 27 of the Evidence Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Except as provided by Section 27 of the Evidence Act, a confession by an accused to a police officer is absolutely protected under Section 25 of the Evidence Act. If the confession is made in the course of an investigation, it is also protected by Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A confession made to any other person by an accused while in the custody of a police officer is protected by Section 26, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. These provisions are based on public policy and must be given the fullest effect.
obiter: Whether a person giving information to a police officer that may be used against them can be deemed to have submitted to the constructive custody of the police officer within the meaning of Section 27 is a point of law on which there is a conflict of opinion.
Section 30 of the Evidence Act, which permits a court to take a confession into consideration against a co-accused, shows that matters affecting other persons may form part of a confession.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's reasoning in the provided text does not address the specific concept of 'constructive custody'. Instead, it establishes the general legal framework that Section 27 of the Evidence Act operates as a proviso that 'partially lifts the ban' imposed by Sections 25 (barring confessions to police) and 26 (barring confessions while in police custody). This exception permits the admission of 'so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered,' but only when that information is received from an accused person who is 'in the custody of a police officer'.
legal_tests_applied: The statutory test from Section 27 of the Evidence Act is applied, which allows information to be proved if: (1) a fact is discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offence, and (2) that person was 'in the custody of a police officer' when giving the information.
why_appellant_lost: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning on this specific issue. It only explains the general legal principle that Section 27 of the Evidence Act creates a statutory exception to the inadmissibility of confessions made to police, which would allow a portion of the appellant's statement to be admitted if the conditions of the section were met.
why_respondent_won: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning on this specific issue. It only lays out the legal rule that Section 27 serves as a proviso to Sections 25 and 26, meaning that if information from an accused in custody leads to a discovery, that specific part of the information is admissible in evidence.
policy_considerations: The general exclusionary rules in Sections 25 and 26 are based on the public policy view that 'confessions made by an accused to a police officer or made by him while he is in the custody of a police officer are not to be trusted, and should not be used in evidence against him.' The court states that the 'fullest effect should be given to them.'
